list.name: namespace
list.label: Instance
list.description: The instance this board reads. Empty on purpose: the chart's templates/grafana-dashboard.yaml replaces this entry with a hidden constant naming the instance it installs, so every namespace="$namespace" selector reads that instance's series and no other. There is no instance picker: each instance ships its own copy of this board, in its own Grafana folder.

list.name: instance
list.label: Instance ID
list.description: The instance ID, used to select this instance's alerts. Empty on purpose: the chart's templates/grafana-dashboard.yaml replaces this entry with a hidden constant holding the ID of the instance it installs.

title: DeviceChain — Messaging
description: Operations board for the message broker and the streams that carry events between services: broker server health, stream size against limits, how far behind each reader is and whether any has lost messages, publishing delays and backpressure, copies and leader changes (including the stream that stores device events arriving over MQTT), failed deliveries and dead letters, and the key-value caches. Broker server panels need the broker's metrics sidecar, which the compact install leaves off. Counts for events that should never happen are shown as a total over the selected time range, so one occurrence stays visible instead of fading into a rate. Each instance gets its own copy of this board, scoped to it.

panels.title: Firing alerts
panels.description: Alerts firing right now for this instance that concern command delivery. An empty table means none are firing. Alerts come from the instance's Prometheus rules, so the table stays empty if those rules are not installed.

panels.title: Broker servers up
panels.description: Message broker servers whose metrics are being collected right now. Fewer than the broker's server count means a server is down or unreachable: check the broker pods first. Reads zero, not an error, when the broker's metrics sidecar is turned off (the compact install turns it off) or when the broker runs outside this instance's namespace.

panels.title: Servers leading the cluster
panels.description: How many broker servers report themselves as the leader of the cluster's stream catalogue. It should read 1. Zero means no leader: streams and consumers cannot be created or changed until one is elected, so check whether a majority of the broker servers are up. More than 1 for longer than a few seconds means the servers disagree, which points at a network split between them. A single-server broker also reads 1.

panels.title: Clients dropped as too slow (range)
panels.description: Clients the broker disconnected in the selected time range because they could not keep up with the messages sent to them. A dropped client lost the messages in flight to it. Check which service restarted or stalled at the time, and whether the broker is short of CPU.

panels.title: Broker requests failing /s
panels.description: Rate of administrative requests to the broker's stream engine that came back as errors (creating a stream or consumer, reading its state). A steady non-zero rate means a service is asking for something the broker refuses. Look at the service logs around the same time.

panels.title: Broker disk in use
panels.description: Highest share of its storage allowance used by any broker server's message store. Stream limits keep this bounded, so a climb towards 100% means streams were sized larger than the disk, or other data is filling it. Add storage or lower the stream limits before it fills.

panels.title: Streams held by the broker
panels.description: How many streams the broker holds, from the most complete server's point of view. A sudden drop means streams were deleted or the broker lost its state.

panels.title: Broker server CPU
panels.description: CPU used by each broker server's process, as a percentage of one core. A server pinned near 100% limits how many messages the instance can move, so add CPU or reduce load before queues build up elsewhere.

panels.title: Broker server memory
panels.description: Memory held by each broker server. It should stay flat. A steady climb with a flat message rate points at a leak, and a server near its memory limit will be restarted, which moves its streams to another server.

panels.title: Client connections
panels.description: Services and devices currently connected to each broker server. After a broker server restarts, its connections should reappear within seconds. A server at zero while the others are busy is not taking its share of traffic.

panels.title: Messages through the broker /s
panels.description: Messages received from and sent to clients and other servers, per broker server. Outgoing exceeding incoming is normal, because each event is read by several services. Use it to see whether a backlog elsewhere coincides with a change in traffic.

panels.title: Connections between broker servers
panels.description: Connections each broker server holds to its peers. The count should be the same on every server and stay steady. A server that drops lower than the others has lost contact with a peer, and streams that depend on that link may be running with fewer copies than configured.

panels.title: Broker disk use over time
panels.description: Share of its storage allowance each broker server's message store is using. See the stat above for what to do when it climbs.

panels.title: Record streams over 80% full
panels.description: Streams that hold failed-message records and dead letters for an operator to read, and that are over 80% of their size or message limit. Nothing processes these streams, so when one reaches its limit the oldest records are discarded unread. Read and clear them, or raise the limit.

targets.expr: count((max by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_stream_used_bytes", namespace="$namespace"} / ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_stream_limit_bytes", namespace="$namespace"} > 0)) > 0.8) and on (stream) (max by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_stream_sink", namespace="$namespace"}) == 1)) or vector(0)

panels.title: Streams refusing new events
panels.description: Streams where the platform is refusing new events so that a slow reader does not lose messages it has not read yet. Every tenant is affected while this is above zero. Find the reader that is behind in the reader panels below and fix or scale it.

panels.title: Events refused (range)
panels.description: Events the platform declined to publish in the selected range because a stream was applying backpressure. Devices or services sending them will see errors or retry. Zero is healthy.

panels.title: Stream fill by size
panels.description: How full each stream is against its size limit. At the limit a stream discards its oldest messages. For streams that hold history this is normal, but a stream whose readers are behind loses messages they have not read yet. The line marks 80%.

panels.title: Stream fill by message count
panels.description: How full each stream is against its message-count limit, for streams that have one. Read it the same way as the size panel beside it.

panels.title: Largest streams on disk
panels.description: The ten biggest streams as the broker itself counts them, including streams the platform did not create, such as the MQTT gateway's own storage. Use it to find what is filling the broker's disk.

panels.title: Messages held per stream
panels.description: Messages currently stored in each of the ten fullest streams, as the broker counts them. A stream that only grows without bound has no limit that fits its traffic.

panels.title: Messages lost unread (range)
panels.description: Messages a reader never processed because the stream discarded them before the reader got to them, in the selected range. These are lost for good. Find the reader in the panels below, restore it, and consider raising the stream's limits.

panels.title: Readers stalled while messages are lost
panels.description: Readers that have been handed nothing while their stream has already discarded messages ahead of them. Each one is losing messages right now. Check that the service reading it is running and not stuck.

targets.expr: count(max by (stream, durable) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_consumer_unread_gap_messages", namespace="$namespace"}) > 0) or vector(0)

panels.title: Messages held past acknowledgement (range)
panels.description: Messages a reader held for longer than the broker waits for an acknowledgement, so the broker handed them out again, in the selected range. The message is processed twice. Repeated occurrences mean a handler is too slow for its deadline.

panels.title: Out-of-attempts notices waiting
panels.description: Notices of messages whose every delivery attempt failed, waiting to be recorded as dead letters. This should drain to zero within seconds. A number that stays above zero means the service that records them is not running.

targets.expr: sum(max by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_stream_used_messages", namespace="$namespace", stream=~".+max-deliveries"})) or vector(0)

panels.title: Unread backlog per reader
panels.description: Messages waiting for each reader that it has not been handed yet. A backlog that grows steadily means the reader is slower than the producers. A brief rise during a restart is normal. Scale the reading service or look for what is slowing it.

panels.title: Handed out, not yet acknowledged
panels.description: Messages each reader has received and not yet confirmed. It normally hovers at the reader's working capacity. A value stuck high means handlers are blocked, and those messages will be handed out again when the wait expires.

panels.title: Share of stream capacity left unread
panels.description: How much of what a stream can hold is still unread by each reader. At 100% the stream discards messages the reader has not seen. Keep this well under 80%. For readers that gate publishing, the stream starts refusing new events at 90%.

panels.title: Messages lost unread /s
panels.description: Rate at which readers are losing messages the stream discarded before they were read, per reader. Any value above zero is data loss. Compare with the backlog panels to see which reader fell behind.

panels.title: Messages waiting to be redelivered
panels.description: Messages the broker has handed out more than once and that are still unacknowledged, per reader, as the broker counts them. A rise means readers are failing or timing out on messages and the broker is retrying them. A message that runs out of attempts becomes a dead letter.

panels.title: Messages held past acknowledgement /s
panels.description: Rate of messages a reader held past the broker's acknowledgement deadline, so they were delivered again. "worker" means a handler was still running. "buffer" means the reader had fetched the message but dropped it before handing it out.

panels.title: Events refused by backpressure /s
panels.description: Rate of events not published because the stream was applying backpressure to protect unread messages. Zero is healthy. A sustained rate means the platform is shedding load: see the capacity panel above for the reader that is behind.

panels.title: Time to publish
panels.description: Time from sending a message to the stream until the broker confirms it. The median should stay in single-digit milliseconds. A rising 99th percentile means the broker is struggling with disk or with copying to other servers, and publishers will start to wait.

panels.title: Share of time publishers wait for the broker
panels.description: How much of the time each publisher had no room to send because it was still waiting for the broker to confirm earlier messages. Anything above a few percent means the broker is the bottleneck for that publisher.

panels.title: Broker layout
panels.description: Whether the broker runs as a cluster or as a single server. A single server stores one copy of everything, so losing it loses the instance's messages until it returns.

panels.title: Streams with fewer copies than configured
panels.description: Streams that the broker holds in fewer copies than this instance is configured for. Until it is back to zero, one more server loss can lose the stream. Check that every broker server is up and connected.

targets.expr: count(max by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_replicas_actual", namespace="$namespace"}) < on (stream) max by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_replicas_desired", namespace="$namespace"})) or vector(0)

panels.title: Streams with copies out of date
panels.description: Streams where fewer copies are caught up and online than the stream has. A copy that is behind cannot take over if the leader fails. It is normal for a moment after a broker server restarts, and a problem if it persists.

targets.expr: count(min by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_peers_current", namespace="$namespace"}) < on (stream) max by (stream) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_replicas_actual", namespace="$namespace"})) or vector(0)

panels.title: Stream leader changes (range)
panels.description: Times any stream changed leader in the selected range. Planned broker restarts cause some. While a stream has no leader, which lasts several seconds, it cannot accept messages.

panels.title: Device-event capture stream leader changes (range)
panels.description: Leader changes, in the selected range, of the stream that stores device events arriving over MQTT. The broker accepts a device's message before this stream stores it, so a change while devices are publishing can lose events the device believes were delivered. Compare the time with the event rate on the ingest side and check which broker server restarted.

panels.title: Readers led from another server
panels.description: Readers whose leader is a different broker server from the one their service is connected to. Each delivery and acknowledgement for them crosses a link between servers, which adds delay. The platform moves them automatically, so a count that stays high is worth a look.

targets.expr: count(max by (stream, durable) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_consumer_leader_local", namespace="$namespace"}) == 0) or vector(0)

panels.title: Copies per stream
panels.description: For every stream and key-value bucket: how many copies are configured, how many the broker reports, and how many are caught up and online. All three should be equal. A lower last column means a copy is behind or its server is down.

panels.title: Stream leader changes
panels.description: Each bar is a leader change seen on a stream. Changes that coincide with a broker restart are expected. Repeated changes without a restart point at an unstable broker or network.

panels.title: Servers that led the MQTT gateway store (selected range)
panels.description: The broker keeps device MQTT messages in its own store, and the platform cannot see that store's leader changes directly. This counts, from the broker's own metrics, how many different servers led it during the selected range. 1 means no change. 2 or more means leadership moved: narrow the range to find when, and see the capture stream stat above.

panels.title: Reader leader moves
panels.description: Times the platform moved a reader's leader to the server its service is connected to. "failed" means the broker refused or did not answer, and nothing changed. A burst of moves follows a broker restart.

panels.title: Dead letters lost (range)
panels.description: Failed messages that could not be written down as dead letters in the selected range, so the record of the failure is gone. Check that the dead-letter stream has room and that the broker accepts writes.

panels.title: Dead letters not saved (range)
panels.description: Dead letters the user-management service received but could not save to its database in the selected range. They stay in the stream and are retried, but a persistent count means the database is unreachable or rejecting them.

panels.title: Silently dead broker connections (range)
panels.description: Times a service dropped a broker connection that had stopped answering without being closed, in the selected range. It is the usual trace of a broker server that was lost or restarted, or of a network split. The service reconnects by itself.

panels.title: Dead letters saved /s
panels.description: Rate at which failed messages are being saved as dead letters by the user-management service. A low steady rate is expected. A sudden jump means something started failing broadly: look at the stage boards for the service that is failing.

panels.title: Messages that ran out of delivery attempts /s
panels.description: Rate of messages whose every delivery attempt failed, by what was done with them. "lettered" means a dead letter was written. "lost" means it could not be written. "replay-covered" means the reader re-reads from its own checkpoint, so nothing is lost, but its checkpoint has not been saving.

panels.title: Broker connections that died silently
panels.description: Broker connections a service dropped because they stopped answering, by service and how it was detected ("ping": the server left pings unanswered; "write": a write made no progress). Several services at once points at the broker or the network rather than at one service.

panels.title: Caches bypassed
panels.description: Caches that are skipping the broker's key-value store because an operation timed out or could not reach it, and are reading the database instead. Reads still work but the database takes the load. Check the broker and the failing-operations panel below.

panels.title: Cache reads answered from memory
panels.description: Share of cache reads served from the service's own memory without asking the broker. A low or falling share means the cache is too small for what is being used, or entries expire before they are reused. Raise the cache size if entries are also being dropped for lack of room.

targets.expr: sum by (cache) (rate({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_kv_cache_local_lookups_total", namespace="$namespace", result="hit"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (cache) (rate({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_kv_cache_local_lookups_total", namespace="$namespace"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Cache memory used
panels.description: How full each cache's in-memory copy is against its byte limit. At the limit it drops the least recently used entries.

panels.title: Entries dropped for lack of room /s
panels.description: Rate at which caches evict entries because they were full. A sustained rate means the cache is smaller than the data being used, so the broker or database is asked more often than needed.

panels.title: Cache operations failing /s
panels.description: Reads and writes to the broker's key-value store that timed out ("timeout") or failed ("error"). After a timeout the cache is bypassed for five seconds. A steady rate means the broker is slow or unreachable for that cache.

panels.title: Cache operation time (99th percentile)
panels.description: Time a cache operation takes at the broker's key-value store, excluding reads answered from memory. Reads are cut off at half a second. A 99th percentile near that cut-off means the store is overloaded.

panels.title: Key-value bucket sizes
panels.description: Size of each key-value bucket on the broker, which stores lease and cache data for the platform. Buckets are small. A bucket that grows without bound is not being cleaned up.
